questions.question_text: According to Amos 7:10-17, what was Amaziah's accusation against Amos, and how did Amos respond?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='20' y='30'>Timeline of Amos and Hosea's Ministries</text></svg>

options.text: Amaziah accused Amos of conspiracy, and Amos denied the accusation, stating he was a prophet by divine call.
Amaziah accused Amos of treason, and Amos responded by prophesying against Amaziah.
Amaziah accused Amos of false prophecy, and Amos justified his prophetic authority.
Amaziah accused Amos of blasphemy, and Amos clarified his message was from God.

questions.explanation: Amaziah accused Amos of conspiring against King Jeroboam II and advised him to flee to Judah (Amos 7:10-13). Amos responded by affirming his divine call to prophesy and delivered a prophecy against Amaziah and his family (Amos 7:14-17).

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Luke 17:11-19, what miracle did Jesus perform when he healed the ten lepers, and what was notable about their response?

options.text: Jesus healed ten lepers, and all returned to thank him.
Jesus healed ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan, returned to thank him.
Jesus healed ten lepers, but none returned to thank him.
Jesus healed one leper, who was a Samaritan, and he returned to thank Jesus.

questions.explanation: Jesus healed ten lepers on his way to Jerusalem. Notably, only one of them, who was a Samaritan, returned to thank Jesus, highlighting the faith of this foreigner among the healed (Luke 17:11-19).

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:42-47, what characterized the daily life of the early Christian community?

options.text: The early Christians were characterized by their individualism and lack of communal activities.
The early Christians devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer.
The early Christians focused solely on prayer and neglected other aspects of community life.
The early Christians were marked by their disunity and frequent disputes.

questions.explanation: The early Christian community was characterized by their devotion to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread (communion), and prayer. They shared their possessions and lived in harmony, enjoying favor with the people (Acts 2:42-47).

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 9:20-22, what miracle did Jesus perform when a woman with a flow of blood touched his cloak, and what was her condition before she touched him?

options.text: The woman was healed instantly and Jesus felt power go out from him.
The woman was rebuked for touching Jesus, but she was healed later.
Jesus ignored the woman, but she was healed after praying.
The woman was cured, but Jesus did not notice it.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 9:20-22, a woman who had been suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years touched the edge of Jesus' cloak and was healed instantly. Jesus felt power go out from him and told the woman that her faith had made her well.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 17:22-31, what was the content of Paul's sermon on the Areopagus in Athens, and how did he address the Athenians' religious practices?

options.text: Paul condemned the Athenians for their idolatry and called them to repentance.
Paul commended the Athenians for their religious devotion and introduced them to Jesus.
Paul used the inscription 'To an Unknown God' as a starting point to preach about the true God.
Paul ignored the Athenians' religious practices and directly preached about Jesus.

questions.explanation: Paul used the Athenians' altar to an unknown god as a point of connection to introduce them to the true God, emphasizing that God is the creator and is not far from humanity.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 1:2-9, what was the significance of Hosea's marriage to Gomer, and what did it symbolize regarding God's relationship with Israel?

options.text: Hosea's marriage symbolized God's faithfulness to Israel despite their unfaithfulness.
Hosea's marriage represented God's judgment on Israel for their idolatry.
Hosea's marriage was a sign of God's love for Israel and their future restoration.
Hosea's marriage was unrelated to God's relationship with Israel.

questions.explanation: Hosea's marriage to Gomer, who was an adulterous woman, symbolized God's relationship with Israel, who were spiritually adulterous. Despite Israel's unfaithfulness, God remained faithful and called them to return to him.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the parable of the talents. According to Matthew 25:14-30, what is the parable teaching about the servants and their master's expectations?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Servants and Talents</text></svg>

options.text: The parable teaches that the servants should have kept the talents safe without investing them.
The parable emphasizes the importance of investing the talents to gain more.
The parable shows that the master was harsh and unfair to the servants.
The parable indicates that the number of talents given was based on the servants' abilities.

questions.explanation: The parable of the talents teaches that the servants are expected to be faithful and productive with the resources entrusted to them. The master commended the servants who invested their talents and gained more, while the unfaithful servant was rebuked for not using his talent wisely.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 4:1-22, what was the reaction of the religious leaders to Peter and John's preaching about Jesus, and what action did they take against them?

options.text: The leaders were convinced by Peter and John and became followers of Jesus.
The leaders arrested Peter and John but released them after being impressed by their courage.
The leaders threatened Peter and John, commanding them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name again.
The leaders ignored Peter and John's message and took no action against them.

questions.explanation: The religious leaders, including the high priest and the Sadducees, were disturbed by Peter and John's preaching about Jesus and the resurrection. They arrested them and commanded them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name again, but Peter and John refused to comply, saying they must obey God rather than men.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 9:32-34, what miracle did Jesus perform when he healed a man who was demon-possessed and mute, and what was the reaction of the crowds?

options.text: The man was healed and the crowds were amazed, saying Jesus was the Son of David.
The man was healed but the crowds were skeptical.
The man was not healed and the crowds were disappointed.
The man was healed and the Pharisees praised Jesus.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 9:32-34, Jesus healed a demon-possessed mute man, and the crowds were amazed, saying, 'Never has anything like this been seen in Israel,' and some said he was the Son of David. The Pharisees, however, attributed his power to Beelzebul.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 9:1-31, what was the account of Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus, and how did it affect his immediate actions?

options.text: Paul was blinded by a light, heard Jesus' voice, and was led into Damascus where he was healed and baptized.
Paul was not affected by the encounter and continued his journey.
Paul was arrested by Roman soldiers on the road.
Paul preached to the disciples in Damascus immediately.

questions.explanation: Acts 9:1-31 describes Paul's conversion where he was blinded by a bright light, heard the voice of Jesus asking why he persecuted him, and was led into Damascus. There, a disciple named Ananias healed and baptized him, after which Paul began to preach.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 5:21-24, what was Amos' attitude towards the religious practices of Israel, and what did he call for?

options.text: Amos rejected their festivals and sacrifices, calling for justice to roll down like waters.
Amos praised their religious practices and encouraged more.
Amos was indifferent to their practices.
Amos suggested they increase their offerings.

questions.explanation: Amos 5:21-24 indicates Amos rejected the religious festivals and sacrifices of Israel because they were not accompanied by justice and righteousness. He called for justice to 'roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream.'

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the parable of the lost sheep. According to Matthew 18:12-14, what is Jesus teaching on the value of one lost sheep, and how does it relate to the Father's will?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Lost Sheep Illustration</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus teaches that the Father does not want any of these little ones to perish.
Jesus teaches that the lost sheep is of no value.
Jesus teaches that the shepherd should leave the lost sheep.
Jesus teaches that only the 99 sheep are important.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 18:12-14, Jesus teaches that the Father does not want 'any of these little ones to perish,' illustrating the value of each individual through the parable of the lost sheep.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:14-36, what was the central message of Peter's sermon on the day of Pentecost, and what was its effect on the listeners?

options.text: Peter preached about Jesus, his death, and resurrection, and the listeners were moved to repentance and baptism.
Peter preached about the law of Moses, and the listeners were confused.
Peter preached about the end times, and the listeners were frightened.
Peter preached about the history of Israel, and the listeners were uninterested.

questions.explanation: Acts 2:14-36 records Peter's sermon on Pentecost, where he preached about Jesus Christ, his crucifixion, and resurrection, citing Psalm 16 and other scriptures. The listeners were deeply moved, repented, and were baptized.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 7:24-27, what is Jesus' teaching on the wise and foolish builders, and what does he emphasize as the foundation for withstanding life's challenges?

options.text: The wise builder is one who hears Jesus' words and acts on them, building on rock.
The foolish builder is one who hears Jesus' words but does not act on them, yet still builds on rock.
The wise builder is one who does not hear Jesus' words but still builds on rock.
The foolish builder is one who hears Jesus' words and acts on them, but builds on sand.

questions.explanation: Jesus teaches that the wise builder is one who hears his words and acts on them, thereby building on a rock that can withstand life's challenges. This is in contrast to the foolish builder who hears but does not act, building on sand. The correct answer reflects Jesus' emphasis on the importance of acting on his teachings.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 4:1-3, what is Amos' criticism of the women of Samaria, and what does he prophesy will happen to them?

options.text: Amos criticizes the women for their idolatry and prophesies their exile.
Amos criticizes the women for their oppression of the poor and prophesies they will be taken away in baskets.
Amos praises the women for their faithfulness and prophesies their prosperity.
Amos criticizes the women for their religious practices and prophesies their restoration.

questions.explanation: Amos criticizes the women of Samaria for their oppression of the poor and their luxurious lifestyle, prophesying that they will be taken away in baskets, likely referring to their being led into exile in a humiliating manner.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a map illustrates Paul's third missionary journey. According to Acts 18:23-19:7, what was the significance of Paul's journey through the Galatian region and Phrygia, and what was his interaction with the disciples in Ephesus?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 50 50 L 100 150 L 200 50 Z' fill='none' stroke='black'/></svg>

options.text: Paul strengthened the disciples in the Galatian region and Phrygia, and then in Ephesus, he found disciples who had only received John's baptism.
Paul established new churches in the Galatian region and Phrygia, and in Ephesus, he baptized disciples in the name of Jesus.
Paul avoided the Galatian region and Phrygia, going directly to Ephesus where he encountered no disciples.
Paul's journey was solely through the Galatian region, with no significant interaction in Ephesus.

questions.explanation: Paul's journey through the Galatian region and Phrygia was significant as he strengthened the disciples. Upon reaching Ephesus, he encountered disciples who had received John's baptism, indicating they were not fully initiated into the Christian faith.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 8:23-27, what miracle did Jesus perform when he calmed the storm, and what was the reaction of the disciples?

options.text: Jesus calmed the storm by speaking to it, and the disciples were amazed and rebuked him for his lack of concern.
Jesus calmed the storm by praying, and the disciples were frightened and questioned his identity.
Jesus calmed the storm by speaking to it, and the disciples were amazed and questioned his authority.
Jesus did not calm the storm, and the disciples were not surprised.

questions.explanation: Jesus performed the miracle of calming the storm by speaking to it, saying 'Peace! Be still!' The disciples were amazed at his authority over nature and questioned who he was.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 4:32-37, what characterized the early Christian community in terms of their possessions and sharing?

options.text: The community held all possessions in common, selling private property to distribute to those in need.
The community kept their possessions private, with no sharing or distribution.
The community shared their possessions occasionally, but maintained private ownership.
The community was characterized by hoarding possessions and not sharing.

questions.explanation: The early Christian community was characterized by a spirit of unity and generosity, where believers held all things in common. They sold their possessions and distributed the proceeds to those in need, demonstrating a radical commitment to sharing and caring for one another.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 8:28-34, what miracle did Jesus perform when he encountered the two demon-possessed men among the tombs, and what was the reaction of the people in the region?

options.text: Jesus healed the men and the people were amazed
Jesus cast out demons into pigs, which then rushed into the sea, and the people begged Jesus to leave
Jesus forgave the men's sins and the people were grateful
Jesus raised the men from the dead and the people were frightened

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 8:28-34, Jesus cast out demons from the two men into a herd of pigs, which then rushed into the sea. The people of the region begged Jesus to leave their area. This event demonstrates Jesus' authority over unclean spirits and the significant impact of his miracles on the local population.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 22:3-16, what was Paul's testimony regarding his background and conversion experience, and how did it relate to his commission to preach to the Gentiles?

options.text: Paul was a Roman citizen by birth and was commissioned to preach to Jews only
Paul was educated at the feet of Gamaliel and was commissioned by the Lord to preach to the Gentiles
Paul persecuted Christians before his conversion and was then commissioned to preach to both Jews and Gentiles
Paul was a Pharisee who never persecuted Christians and was called to preach to Gentiles after his conversion

questions.explanation: Acts 22:3-16 details Paul's testimony about being a Pharisee educated by Gamaliel, his persecution of Christians, his conversion experience on the road to Damascus, and his subsequent commission to preach to the Gentiles. This passage highlights Paul's transformation from a persecutor to a preacher of the Gospel.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 8:4-7, what was Amos' criticism of the Israelites, and what did he prophesy would happen to them because of their actions?

options.text: Amos criticized Israel for their idolatry and prophesied their exile
Amos condemned Israel for their social injustice and prophesied famine
Amos denounced Israel for their religious hypocrisy and prophesied a day of darkness
Amos rebuked Israel for their lack of faith and prophesied destruction

questions.explanation: Amos 8:4-7 records Amos' condemnation of Israel for their exploitation of the needy and their religious hypocrisy. He prophesied a day of darkness and famine as a consequence of their actions. This passage highlights Amos' concern for social justice and the integrity of worship.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the parable of the sower. According to Matthew 13:1-23, what does Jesus teach about the different types of soil and their responses to the seed?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><path d='M50,50 L70,70' stroke='black'/><text x='100' y='50'>Seed</text></svg>

options.text: The parable teaches about four types of soil representing different responses to the Gospel: the path, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil
The parable describes three types of soil: fertile, barren, and rocky
The parable illustrates two types of soil: good and bad
The parable explains the process of sowing seeds in different conditions

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 13:1-23, Jesus teaches about four types of soil in the parable of the sower: the path where the seed is eaten by birds, rocky ground where it withers, thorny ground where it is choked, and good soil where it produces fruit. This parable illustrates different responses to the message of the Kingdom.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 6:1-7, what was the problem that arose in the early Christian community regarding the distribution of food, and how was it resolved?

options.text: The problem was between Hebrew-speaking and Greek-speaking widows, resolved by the appointment of seven men to serve tables
The issue was about sharing possessions, resolved by selling goods and distributing to all
The conflict was between apostles and other believers, resolved by the apostles taking charge of distribution
The problem was about the lack of food, resolved by praying for more resources

questions.explanation: Acts 6:1-7 describes a complaint by Greek-speaking Jews against Hebrew-speaking Jews regarding the neglect of their widows in the daily distribution of food. The apostles proposed appointing seven men to oversee this task, thus resolving the issue and allowing the apostles to focus on prayer and the ministry of the word.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 15:21-28, what miracle did Jesus perform for the Canaanite woman's daughter, and what was notable about their interaction?

options.text: Jesus initially refused to help, then healed the daughter due to the woman's faith.
Jesus directly healed the daughter without any interaction with the woman.
The woman was criticized by Jesus for her lack of faith.
The healing occurred without the woman's request.

questions.explanation: Jesus initially responded to the Canaanite woman by saying he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, but the woman persisted, saying even dogs eat crumbs from their master's table. Jesus commended her faith and healed her daughter. This interaction highlights Jesus' initial reluctance to help a Gentile and the woman's persistent faith.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 20:17-38, what was the content of Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders, and what was its significance?

options.text: Paul warned them about false teachers and commended their faithfulness.
Paul instructed them to abandon their mission and return to Jerusalem.
Paul focused solely on his own conversion experience.
Paul advised them to persecute the local Christians.

questions.explanation: Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders included warnings about false teachers who would arise from among them and from outside, and he commended their faithfulness, recalling his ministry among them. This address is significant as it shows Paul's concern for the future of the church and his care for the leaders he had mentored.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 9:11-15, what is Amos' prophecy regarding the restoration of Israel, and what does it entail?

options.text: Amos prophesied that Israel would be completely destroyed and never restored.
Amos prophesied the rebuilding of the fallen booth of David and Israel's possession of the remnant of Edom.
Amos focused solely on the judgment of Israel without mentioning restoration.
The prophecy was limited to the northern kingdom only.

questions.explanation: Amos 9:11-15 prophesies the restoration of Israel, including the rebuilding of the fallen booth of David, and Israel's possession of the remnant of Edom. This passage looks forward to a future time of restoration and blessing for Israel, indicating a hopeful future beyond judgment.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the parable of the weeds among the wheat. According to Matthew 13:24-30, what does Jesus teach about the kingdom of heaven through this parable?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Wheat and Weeds</text></svg>

options.text: The kingdom is to be separated immediately from evil.
The kingdom allows both good and evil to coexist until the harvest.
The parable teaches that only the righteous will be in the kingdom.
The parable emphasizes the destruction of the wicked.

questions.explanation: The parable of the weeds among the wheat teaches that the kingdom of heaven is like a field where wheat and weeds grow together. Jesus explains that the weeds should not be pulled out until the harvest to avoid harming the wheat, illustrating that good and evil coexist in the world until the final judgment.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:1-4, what event occurred on the day of Pentecost, and what was its significance for the early Christians?

options.text: The disciples were scattered due to persecution.
The Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, enabling them to speak in different languages.
Peter delivered a sermon that was met with hostility.
The early Christians decided to abandon their mission.

questions.explanation: On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, and they were filled with the Spirit, enabling them to speak in different languages. This event was significant as it empowered the disciples for their mission to spread the gospel to people from various nations gathered in Jerusalem.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:13-16, what is Jesus' teaching on the role of his disciples in the world, and how are they to influence others?

options.text: Jesus teaches that his disciples are to be like salt that loses its saltiness and light that is hidden under a bushel.
Jesus teaches that his disciples are to be like salt that preserves and light that shines before others to glorify God.
Jesus teaches that his disciples are to be like salt that is thrown away and light that is extinguished.
Jesus teaches that his disciples are to be like salt that is preserved and light that is hidden.

questions.explanation: Jesus teaches that his disciples are to be the salt of the earth and the light of the world. They are to preserve and influence others positively, just like salt preserves food and light illuminates darkness. This is evident in Matthew 5:13-16 where Jesus emphasizes the importance of being a positive influence.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 16:9-10, what was the vision that Paul had during his second missionary journey, and how did it influence his travels?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Map of Paul's Second Missionary Journey</text></svg>

options.text: Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia calling for help, which led him to travel to Macedonia.
Paul had a vision of a man from Asia calling for help, which led him to travel to Asia.
Paul had a vision of Jesus commanding him to stay in Asia, which led him to remain there.
Paul had a vision of an angel telling him to return to Jerusalem.

questions.explanation: According to Acts 16:9-10, Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia calling for help. This vision led Paul to conclude that God was calling him to preach the gospel in Macedonia, thus influencing his travels during the second missionary journey.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 3:1-2, what was Amos' message to the Israelites regarding their relationship with God, and what did he emphasize?

options.text: Amos emphasized that God had a special relationship with the Israelites and would punish them for their sins.
Amos emphasized that God had no special relationship with the Israelites and would ignore their sins.
Amos emphasized that God had chosen the Israelites but would not hold them accountable for their actions.
Amos emphasized that God's relationship with the Israelites was the same as with other nations.

questions.explanation: Amos 3:1-2 highlights Amos' message that God had a special relationship with the Israelites, having chosen them from all the families of the earth. Because of this unique relationship, God would punish them for their sins, emphasizing accountability due to their covenant with Him.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 14:22-33, what miracle did Jesus perform when he walked on the water, and what was the reaction of the disciples?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Illustration of Jesus Walking on Water</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus calmed the storm, and the disciples were amazed and worshiped him.
Jesus walked on the water, and the disciples were terrified, thinking he was a ghost.
Jesus sailed across the sea, and the disciples were relieved.
Jesus stayed on the shore, and the disciples were confused.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 14:22-33, Jesus performed the miracle of walking on the water. The disciples were initially terrified, thinking he was a ghost. However, upon Jesus' reassurance, they worshiped him, recognizing his divine power.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:1-4, what event occurred on the day of Pentecost, and what was its significance for the early Christian community?

options.text: The day of Pentecost marked the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples, empowering them for their mission.
The day of Pentecost marked the beginning of Paul's missionary journeys.
The day of Pentecost was a day of fasting and mourning for the early Christians.
The day of Pentecost was ignored by the early Christian community.

questions.explanation: The event on the day of Pentecost, as described in Acts 2:1-4, was the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. This event empowered them for their mission, enabling them to speak in different languages and boldly proclaim the gospel, marking a significant moment in the establishment of the early Christian community.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:38-42, what is Jesus' teaching on retaliation and generosity, and what does he emphasize as the appropriate Christian response to being wronged?

options.text: Jesus teaches to retaliate with equal measure and to be generous only to those who are kind.
Jesus teaches not to resist an evildoer and to go the extra mile for someone who forces you to go one mile.
Jesus advocates for violent retaliation against evildoers and being stingy with one's resources.
Jesus emphasizes the importance of turning the other cheek and giving to everyone who asks.

questions.explanation: Jesus teaches his followers not to resist an evildoer and to be generous beyond the immediate demand, illustrating a principle of non-retaliation and extraordinary kindness.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 13:4-12, what was the outcome of Paul's preaching in Cyprus, and how did the proconsul Sergius Paulus respond?

options.text: Paul was rejected, and Sergius Paulus persecuted him.
Paul was successful in his preaching, and Sergius Paulus was amazed by the miracle performed by Paul.
Paul was imprisoned, and Sergius Paulus was indifferent to his message.
Paul preached but had no significant impact, and Sergius Paulus remained unchanged.

questions.explanation: Paul's preaching in Cyprus resulted in the conversion of Sergius Paulus after Paul struck Elymas with temporary blindness, demonstrating the power of God's word.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 7:1-9, what were the visions that Amos received from God regarding Israel's fate, and what did they signify?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Diagram illustrating Amos' visions</text></svg>

options.text: The visions foretold Israel's prosperity and peace.
The visions included locusts, fire, and a plumb line, signifying God's judgment on Israel.
The visions were about the restoration of Jerusalem.
The visions concerned the conquest of Canaan.

questions.explanation: Amos received visions that included locusts, fire, and a plumb line, which signified God's judgment and impending destruction on Israel due to their sins.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 9:1-8, what miracle did Jesus perform when he healed the paralytic man, and what was the reaction of the Pharisees?

options.text: Jesus forgave the man's sins, and the Pharisees praised him.
Jesus healed the man physically, and the Pharisees were amazed.
Jesus forgave the man's sins, and the Pharisees accused him of blasphemy.
Jesus ignored the man, and the Pharisees were indifferent.

questions.explanation: Jesus forgave the paralytic man's sins, which led to the Pharisees accusing him of blasphemy, as they believed only God could forgive sins.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:42-47, what characterized the daily life of the early Christian community, and how did they interact with one another?

options.text: They were characterized by division and selfishness.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, and sharing, living in harmony.
They focused solely on prayer and ignored other aspects of community life.
They were marked by indifference to one another's needs.

questions.explanation: The early Christians were devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer, demonstrating a strong sense of community and sharing.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:21-22, what is Jesus' teaching on anger and reconciliation, and what does he emphasize as the condition for being reconciled to God?

options.text: Jesus teaches that anger is not a sin and reconciliation is not necessary.
Jesus emphasizes that being reconciled to one's brother is a condition for being reconciled to God.
Jesus says that reconciliation is only necessary with those who have wronged us.
Jesus teaches that forgiveness is not necessary if the other person does not apologize.

questions.explanation: Jesus teaches that being angry with one's brother without cause is akin to being guilty before the divine court, and emphasizes the importance of reconciliation before offering a gift at the altar (Matthew 5:21-24). Thus, being reconciled to one's brother is a condition for being reconciled to God.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 7:10-17, what was Amos' confrontation with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, and what was the outcome?

options.text: Amos was welcomed by Amaziah and allowed to continue prophesying.
Amos was accused of conspiracy and told to flee to Judah.
Amaziah accused Amos of treason against Jeroboam, and Amos prophesied against Amaziah's family.
Amos and Amaziah had a friendly discussion about the prophecies.

questions.explanation: Amaziah accused Amos of conspiring against Jeroboam and told him to flee to Judah. Amos responded by prophesying against Amaziah's family, foretelling their exile and the downfall of Israel (Amos 7:10-17).

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a map illustrates Paul's second missionary journey. According to Acts 16:9-15, what was the significance of Paul's vision of the man from Macedonia, and how did it influence his missionary journey? In the diagram below, ...
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M100,100 L150,150' stroke='black'/></svg>

options.text: The vision led Paul to continue his journey in Asia Minor.
The vision directed Paul to preach in Macedonia.
The vision resulted in Paul returning to Jerusalem.
The vision had no impact on Paul's journey.

questions.explanation: Paul's vision of the man from Macedonia was a call to preach the gospel in Macedonia. This vision led Paul and his companions to cross over into Macedonia, marking a significant shift in their missionary journey (Acts 16:9-10).

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 9:20-22, what miracle did Jesus perform when a woman with a bleeding disorder touched his cloak, and what was the significance of her faith?

options.text: Jesus healed the woman because of her wealth.
The woman was healed due to her faith in touching Jesus' cloak.
Jesus did not notice the woman and she was not healed.
The miracle was performed because the woman was a relative of Jesus.

questions.explanation: The woman was healed because of her faith. Jesus noted that it was her faith that saved her, saying 'your faith has made you well' (Matthew 9:22).

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:5-12, what was notable about the crowd that witnessed the event of Pentecost, and how did they respond?

options.text: The crowd was entirely Jewish and they were confused by the languages spoken.
The crowd was from various nations and they heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
The crowd was hostile and immediately persecuted the disciples.
The crowd was indifferent and left without any response.

questions.explanation: The crowd at Pentecost was composed of people from various nations, who were amazed to hear the disciples speaking in their own languages about the wonders of God (Acts 2:5-12).

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:43-48, what is Jesus' teaching on loving one's neighbors and enemies, and what does he emphasize as the characteristic of his disciples?

options.text: Jesus teaches that loving one's neighbors is sufficient, and his disciples should focus on being kind to those they know.
Jesus emphasizes that his disciples should love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, to be like their heavenly Father who is perfect.
Jesus instructs his disciples to love their neighbors but hate their enemies, to maintain a balance in their relationships.
Jesus says that loving one's enemies is optional, but it is mandatory to love one's neighbors.

questions.explanation: Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:43-48 emphasizes the importance of loving not just one's neighbors but also one's enemies. He stresses that this behavior is characteristic of his disciples and reflects the perfection of their heavenly Father. The correct answer highlights this teaching and its significance.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 9:1-31, what was the significance of Paul's conversion experience on the road to Damascus, and how did it impact his mission?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M50,100 L270,100' stroke='black' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='20' fill='blue'/></svg>

options.text: Paul's conversion led him to continue persecuting Christians, but with a new strategy.
Paul became a disciple and a key figure in spreading Christianity, despite initial skepticism from the disciples.
Paul's experience had no significant impact on his life or mission.
Paul immediately began his missionary journeys without any preparation or support from the early Christian community.

questions.explanation: Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus was a pivotal event that transformed him from a persecutor of Christians to a key figure in spreading Christianity. Initially, there was skepticism among the disciples, but he eventually became a crucial part of the early Christian mission. The diagram illustrates the road to Damascus.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 5:21-24, what was Amos' criticism of the Israelites' religious practices, and what did he emphasize as more important?

options.text: Amos praised the Israelites for their religious festivals and sacrifices, emphasizing their importance.
Amos criticized the Israelites for neglecting their religious practices, urging them to do more.
Amos condemned the Israelites' religious practices as empty and hypocritical, emphasizing the need for justice and righteousness.
Amos suggested that the Israelites should adopt new religious practices to replace their existing ones.

questions.explanation: Amos 5:21-24 highlights Amos' criticism of the Israelites' religious practices, describing them as empty and hypocritical. He emphasizes that what God truly desires is justice and righteousness, not mere religious rituals.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 9:32-34, what miracle did Jesus perform when he healed a demon-possessed man, and what was the reaction of the crowds?

options.text: Jesus healed a blind man, and the crowds were amazed.
Jesus healed a demon-possessed man, and the crowds were astonished but the Pharisees attributed it to Beelzebul.
Jesus raised a dead person, and the crowds mourned.
Jesus cleansed a leper, and the crowds were indifferent.

questions.explanation: The miracle in Matthew 9:32-34 involves Jesus healing a demon-possessed man. The crowds were astonished by this miracle, but the Pharisees reacted negatively, attributing Jesus' power to Beelzebul.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:14-21, what was Peter's message regarding the event of Pentecost, and what did he cite as its fulfillment?

options.text: Peter explained that Pentecost was a natural phenomenon with no spiritual significance.
Peter cited Joel's prophecy, stating that Pentecost was a fulfillment of God's promise to pour out His Spirit on all people.
Peter attributed Pentecost to human actions and efforts.
Peter said that Pentecost was a sign of judgment rather than a blessing.

questions.explanation: Peter's message in Acts 2:14-21 interprets the event of Pentecost as a fulfillment of Joel's prophecy. He explains that it is a sign of God pouring out His Spirit on all people, marking a significant moment in the early Christian community.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 13:31-32, what is the significance of the parable of the mustard seed in Jesus' teaching, and what does it reveal about the kingdom of heaven?

options.text: The parable of the mustard seed illustrates the rapid and expansive growth of the kingdom of heaven from small beginnings.
The parable of the mustard seed teaches that the kingdom of heaven is only for those who are already members of the Jewish community.
The parable of the mustard seed is a warning against the dangers of pride and arrogance in the community of believers.
The parable of the mustard seed signifies the end times and the final judgment.

questions.explanation: The parable of the mustard seed, as explained by Jesus in Matthew 13:31-32, highlights the kingdom of heaven's growth from small, seemingly insignificant beginnings to something large and expansive. This parable is meant to illustrate the surprising and expansive nature of God's kingdom. Thus, option A is the correct interpretation. Options B, C, and D misinterpret the parable's significance.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 17:16-34, what was Paul's message to the Athenians, and how did they respond?

options.text: Paul preached about the unknown god, emphasizing the resurrection of Jesus, and some Athenians believed while others mocked him.
Paul spoke about the history of Israel, and the Athenians were unanimous in their acceptance of his message.
Paul discussed the philosophy of Stoicism, and the Athenians were deeply moved to repentance.
Paul condemned the idolatry of Athens, and the city council immediately expelled him.

questions.explanation: In Acts 17:16-34, Paul's message to the Athenians at the Areopagus focused on the unknown god, leading to his proclamation of the God of the Bible and the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The response was mixed, with some mocking and others believing. This matches the description in option A. Options B, C, and D inaccurately represent Paul's message and the Athenians' response.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 6:1-3, what is Hosea's call to the Israelites, and what does it reveal about God's character?

options.text: Hosea calls the Israelites to repentance, highlighting God's desire for mercy and knowledge of God rather than mere ritual.
Hosea commands the Israelites to offer more sacrifices to appease God's wrath.
Hosea prophesies the total destruction of Israel without any hope of restoration.
Hosea emphasizes the importance of observing religious festivals strictly.

questions.explanation: Hosea 6:1-3 presents a call to the Israelites to return to God, emphasizing the importance of genuine repentance and the pursuit of knowledge of God. This passage highlights God's character as one who desires mercy and a personal relationship with His people. Thus, option A accurately reflects the passage's message. Options B, C, and D misrepresent Hosea's call and God's character.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the healing of the blind man. According to John 9:1-41, what miracle did Jesus perform, and what was its significance?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Healing of the Blind Man</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus healed a man born blind, demonstrating His power over physical blindness and spiritual darkness.
Jesus cured a man with a fever, showing His authority over illness.
Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead, signifying His power over death itself.
Jesus calmed a storm, illustrating His control over nature.

questions.explanation: The miracle described in John 9:1-41 is the healing of a man born blind. Jesus' action not only restored the man's physical sight but also served as a sign to reveal God's glory and Jesus' identity as the Light of the World. Thus, option A is the correct interpretation. Options B, C, and D refer to different miracles performed by Jesus.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 4:32-37, what characterized the early Christian community in Jerusalem, and what was the significance of Barnabas' action?

options.text: The community was marked by unity and generosity, with Barnabas selling his land and donating the proceeds to the apostles.
The community was divided, with Barnabas being a key figure in resolving conflicts.
The community was primarily concerned with missionary work outside Jerusalem, led by Barnabas.
The community was focused on doctrinal debates, with Barnabas advocating for a strict adherence to Jewish law.

questions.explanation: Acts 4:32-37 describes the early Christian community as being characterized by a remarkable unity and generosity among its members. Barnabas is highlighted as an example of this generosity when he sold a field he owned and brought the money to the apostles. This act exemplifies the community's spirit of sharing and caring for one another. Thus, option A accurately describes the scene. Options B, C, and D misrepresent the characteristics of the early community and Barnabas' role.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 13:44-46, what are the parables that Jesus used to describe the kingdom of heaven, and what do they signify?

options.text: The parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl of great price signify the kingdom's value and worth seeking.
The parables of the sower and the soils signify the different responses to Jesus' teachings.
The parables of the lost sheep and the prodigal son signify God's love and mercy.
The parables of the talents and the pounds signify the importance of stewardship.

questions.explanation: Jesus used the parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl of great price to illustrate the immense value of the kingdom of heaven, emphasizing that it is worth sacrificing everything to attain. This is in line with Matthew 13:44-46, where Jesus describes these parables.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 22:1-21, what was Paul's defense before the crowd in Jerusalem, and what was the significance of his conversion experience?

options.text: Paul's defense emphasized his persecution of Christians before his conversion and his subsequent call to preach to the Gentiles.
Paul's defense focused on his Pharisaic background and his zeal for the law.
Paul's defense highlighted his role in the stoning of Stephen.
Paul's defense detailed his missionary journeys and the churches he established.

questions.explanation: Paul's defense before the crowd in Jerusalem, as recorded in Acts 22:1-21, centered on his conversion experience and his call to preach to the Gentiles. He recounted his past as a persecutor of Christians and how God called him to a new mission.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 11:1-4, what is Hosea's description of God's relationship with Israel, and what does it reveal about God's character?

options.text: Hosea describes God's relationship with Israel as one of love and care, revealing God's compassionate character.
Hosea portrays God's relationship with Israel as strictly judgmental, highlighting God's justice.
Hosea depicts God's relationship with Israel as distant and uninvolved.
Hosea illustrates God's relationship with Israel as conditional upon their obedience.

questions.explanation: Hosea 11:1-4 illustrates God's love and care for Israel, comparing it to a father's love for his child. This passage reveals God's character as compassionate and nurturing.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the healing of a blind man. According to John 9:1-7, what miracle did Jesus perform, and what was notable about the method he used?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Blind Man Healing</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus healed the blind man by touching his eyes, demonstrating physical contact was necessary.
Jesus healed the blind man by making clay and applying it to his eyes, followed by washing in the Pool of Siloam.
Jesus healed the blind man through a prayer, showing the power of intercession.
Jesus healed the blind man by simply declaring him healed, demonstrating his authority.

questions.explanation: According to John 9:1-7, Jesus healed the blind man by making clay with his saliva, applying it to the man's eyes, and then instructing him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. This method was notable for its uniqueness and the requirement for the man to obey Jesus' instructions.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 4:32-35, what characterized the early Christian community in Jerusalem, and what was the significance of their practices?

options.text: The early Christian community was characterized by unity and generosity, sharing their possessions to meet each other's needs.
The early Christian community was marked by division and conflict over resources.
The early Christian community focused on missionary work, sending out apostles to preach.
The early Christian community was isolated, having little interaction with the wider Jewish community.

questions.explanation: Acts 4:32-35 describes the early Christian community as being characterized by unity and a generous spirit, where believers shared their possessions to ensure that no one among them was in need. This practice highlighted their commitment to caring for one another.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 7:24-27, what is Jesus' teaching on the wise and foolish builders, and what does it reveal about the importance of his teachings?

options.text: The parable emphasizes the importance of faith in Jesus.
The parable highlights the need to follow Jesus' teachings to build a strong spiritual foundation.
The parable illustrates the consequences of not loving one's neighbors.
The parable teaches about the coming judgment and the need for repentance.

questions.explanation: Jesus' teaching on the wise and foolish builders emphasizes the importance of putting his words into practice. The wise builder, who builds on rock, represents those who hear and obey Jesus' teachings, while the foolish builder, who builds on sand, represents those who hear but do not obey. This parable highlights the significance of following Jesus' teachings to establish a strong spiritual foundation.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 9:36-43, what miracle did Peter perform in Joppa, and what was its significance for the early Christian community?

options.text: Peter raised Tabitha from the dead, demonstrating God's power and compassion.
Peter healed a man with a bleeding disorder, showcasing Jesus' healing power.
Peter preached to the Gentiles, marking the beginning of the Gentile mission.
Peter resolved a dispute among the apostles, establishing a precedent for church leadership.

questions.explanation: In Acts 9:36-43, Peter raises Tabitha (Dorcas) from the dead. This miracle demonstrates God's power and compassion, and it has a significant impact on the early Christian community in Joppa, as it showcases the continuation of Jesus' ministry through his disciples.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 2:14-23, what is Hosea's description of God's restoration of Israel, and what does it reveal about God's character?

options.text: God's restoration involves punishment and judgment.
God's restoration is characterized by love, compassion, and renewal.
God's restoration is conditional upon Israel's repentance.
God's restoration is limited to the faithful remnant.

questions.explanation: Hosea 2:14-23 describes God's restoration of Israel as an act of love and compassion. God speaks of wooing Israel, leading her into the wilderness, and speaking tenderly to her, promising to give her vineyards and to make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. This passage reveals God's character as one of love, mercy, and faithfulness, highlighting his desire to restore and renew his relationship with his people.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the healing of a paralytic. According to Luke 5:17-26, what miracle did Jesus perform, and what was the reaction of the Pharisees and teachers of the law? <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Healing of Paralytic</text></svg>
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Healing of Paralytic</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus healed the paralytic, and the Pharisees praised his divine authority.
Jesus forgave the paralytic's sins, and the Pharisees accused him of blasphemy.
Jesus taught the crowd, and the Pharisees questioned his interpretation of the law.
Jesus performed an exorcism, and the Pharisees attributed it to Beelzebul.

questions.explanation: According to Luke 5:17-26, Jesus healed a paralytic man, first forgiving his sins, which led the Pharisees and teachers of the law to accuse him of blasphemy, as they believed that only God could forgive sins. Jesus then healed the man to demonstrate his authority to forgive sins, challenging their accusations.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 4:1-22, what was the reaction of the religious leaders to Peter and John's preaching about Jesus, and what did they ultimately decide to do?

options.text: The leaders arrested Peter and John, then released them with a warning not to preach again.
The leaders imprisoned Peter and John, but they were miraculously released.
The leaders interrogated Peter and John, then decided to let them go after being impressed by their courage.
The leaders stoned Peter and John for blasphemy.

questions.explanation: In Acts 4:1-22, after Peter and John healed a lame man and preached about Jesus, the religious leaders (including the Sadducees and the captain of the temple guard) arrested them. After interrogating them, they were impressed by their courage and the evidence of the miracle. They decided to release them with a warning not to speak or teach in the name of Jesus again. However, Peter and John responded that they could not help but speak about what they had seen and heard.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 7:7-8, what is Jesus' teaching on prayer, and what does he emphasize as the condition for receiving an answer?

options.text: Jesus teaches that one should pray with persistence and emphasizes that everyone who asks receives.
Jesus teaches that one should pray with humility and emphasizes that only the righteous receive an answer.
Jesus teaches that one should pray with faith and emphasizes that God gives good gifts to those who ask.
Jesus teaches that one should pray with fasting and emphasizes that the answer comes only after trials.

questions.explanation: Jesus' teaching on prayer in Matthew 7:7-8 emphasizes asking, seeking, and knocking as means to receive an answer from God. He assures that everyone who asks receives, and who seeks finds, and to who knocks, the door will be opened. The condition for receiving an answer is having faith and persistence in prayer, and God is portrayed as a generous giver of good gifts.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 16:16-18, what miracle did Paul perform when he encountered a slave girl with a spirit of divination, and what was the reaction of her owners?

options.text: Paul healed the girl, and her owners were grateful for the miracle.
Paul cast out the spirit, and her owners were angry because their profit was lost.
Paul preached to the girl, and her owners were indifferent to the outcome.
Paul ignored the girl, and her owners were unaffected by his actions.

questions.explanation: In Acts 16:16-18, Paul encounters a slave girl with a spirit of divination who was being used by her owners for profit through fortune-telling. Paul casts out the spirit, freeing her from her condition. The owners react with anger because their source of profit is lost. This event highlights Paul's authority over evil spirits and the tension between the early Christian mission and the economic interests of those opposed to it.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 4:1-3, what is Hosea's criticism of the Israelites, and what does he emphasize as the consequence of their actions?

options.text: Hosea criticizes the Israelites for their idolatry and emphasizes that their actions will lead to famine and desolation.
Hosea criticizes the Israelites for their social injustice and emphasizes that their actions will lead to military defeat.
Hosea criticizes the Israelites for their lack of faith and emphasizes that their actions will lead to spiritual barrenness.
Hosea criticizes the Israelites for their ritual practices and emphasizes that their actions will lead to divine approval.

questions.explanation: Hosea 4:1-3 criticizes the Israelites for their lack of faithfulness, knowledge of God, and their involvement in swearing, lying, and killing. Hosea emphasizes that these actions have led to a breakdown in societal norms and a consequent desolation of the land, affecting both the people and the animals. The passage highlights the interconnectedness of the people's spiritual condition and the natural world's state.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a graphic illustrates the healing of a leper. According to Matthew 8:1-4, what miracle did Jesus perform when he encountered a man with leprosy, and what was Jesus' instruction to the healed man?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='none' stroke='black'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Jesus healing a leper</text></svg>

options.text: Jesus healed the leper and instructed him to tell everyone about the miracle.
Jesus healed the leper and instructed him to show himself to the priest and offer the gift commanded by Moses.
Jesus preached to the leper and instructed him to follow him.
Jesus ignored the leper and continued on his journey.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 8:1-4, Jesus heals a man with leprosy by touching him and saying, 'Be clean.' Jesus then instructs the healed man to show himself to the priest and offer the gift commanded by Moses, as a testimony to the priests and the community, and to follow the law. This miracle demonstrates Jesus' power and compassion, and his respect for the Mosaic law.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:1-4, what was the significance of the event of Pentecost for the disciples, and how did it manifest?

options.text: The event of Pentecost marked the beginning of the disciples' mission, manifesting as a loud noise and tongues of fire.
The event of Pentecost was a time of prayer and fasting for the disciples, manifesting as a quiet reflection.
The event of Pentecost was a celebration of the harvest, manifesting as feasting and rejoicing.
The event of Pentecost was a moment of doubt and fear for the disciples, manifesting as hiding and isolation.

questions.explanation: Acts 2:1-4 describes the event of Pentecost, where the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit. The event is marked by a sudden loud noise like a violent wind and the appearance of tongues of fire that rest on each of the disciples. They are then enabled to speak in different languages, allowing them to communicate with people from various nations present in Jerusalem. This event signifies the empowerment of the disciples for their mission to spread the Gospel to all nations.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 6:9-13, what is Jesus' model prayer, and what elements does it emphasize as essential for a disciple's prayer life?

options.text: The Lord's Prayer emphasizes forgiveness, daily bread, and hallowing God's name.
The Lord's Prayer focuses on personal petitions, material wealth, and divine judgment.
The Lord's Prayer includes reverence for God, a request for daily provision, and a plea for forgiveness.
The Lord's Prayer is centered on fasting, prayer rituals, and the pursuit of righteousness.

questions.explanation: Jesus' model prayer, known as the Lord's Prayer, is recorded in Matthew 6:9-13. It begins with addressing God as 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name' (reverence), followed by 'Give us today our daily bread' (request for daily provision), and 'And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (plea for forgiveness). This structure emphasizes the importance of revering God, seeking daily provision, and practicing forgiveness in a disciple's prayer life.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to 1 Samuel 17:1-58, what was the significance of David's confrontation with Goliath, and how did it impact his relationship with King Saul?

options.text: David's victory over Goliath led to his immediate appointment as a high-ranking military officer under King Saul.
David's confrontation with Goliath was a test of his faith, and his victory earned him recognition and a close relationship with King Saul initially.
David's defeat of Goliath resulted in his exile from Israel and a complete breakdown in his relationship with King Saul.
David's victory over Goliath was seen as a minor event with little impact on his future or his relationship with King Saul.

questions.explanation: David's confrontation with Goliath, as described in 1 Samuel 17, was a pivotal moment that showcased his faith in God. His victory over the giant Philistine warrior not only saved Israel but also brought David to the attention of King Saul. Initially, David became a close companion to Saul, with Saul's son Jonathan forming a significant bond with him (1 Samuel 18:1-4). However, Saul's growing jealousy and fear of David's rising popularity eventually strained their relationship.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a map illustrates Paul's first missionary journey. According to Acts 13:4-12, what was the significance of Paul's ministry in Cyprus, and how did it reflect his missionary strategy?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M50,50 L270,50' stroke='black'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='20' fill='blue'/></svg>

options.text: Paul's ministry in Cyprus was focused on Jewish synagogues, reflecting his strategy to start with Jewish communities.
Paul's work in Cyprus was primarily among Gentiles, demonstrating a shift away from Jewish audiences.
Paul's mission in Cyprus was marked by a confrontation with a Roman proconsul, Sergius Paulus, who became a believer.
Paul's journey to Cyprus was solely for the purpose of establishing trade routes for the early Christian community.

questions.explanation: Acts 13:4-12 describes Paul's first missionary journey, which included a significant stop in Cyprus. There, Paul encountered Elymas, a magician, and confronted him before Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul. Sergius Paulus became a believer after witnessing Paul's rebuke of Elymas (Acts 13:7, 12). This event not only highlights Paul's boldness and the power of the gospel but also demonstrates his ability to engage with high-ranking officials, reflecting a strategic approach to spreading Christianity among influential people.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to John 6:1-14, what miracle did Jesus perform when he fed a large crowd with a few loaves of bread and some fish, and what was the crowd's response?

options.text: Jesus fed the crowd by miraculously multiplying the bread and fish, and the crowd recognized him as the Messiah.
Jesus used the available bread and fish to teach the crowd about the importance of sharing.
The miracle of feeding the crowd was performed by Jesus' disciples, not Jesus himself.
The crowd was skeptical and unresponsive to Jesus' miracle of feeding them.

questions.explanation: The feeding of the 5,000 is a well-documented miracle of Jesus, recorded in all four Gospels, including John 6:1-14. Jesus took five loaves of bread and two fish, blessed them, and they were miraculously multiplied to feed a large crowd. The crowd's response was to recognize Jesus as a prophet and attempt to make him king (John 6:14-15), indicating their understanding of him as the Messiah.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Hosea 1:2-9, what was the significance of Hosea's marriage to Gomer, and how did it symbolize God's relationship with Israel?

options.text: Hosea's marriage to Gomer symbolized God's faithful and loving covenant with Israel despite Israel's unfaithfulness.
Hosea's marriage was a literal example of the ideal family life advocated by the prophets.
The marriage was a metaphor for the coming exile and the destruction of Israel.
Hosea's marriage to Gomer was unrelated to his prophetic message about God's relationship with Israel.

questions.explanation: Hosea's marriage to Gomer, as described in Hosea 1:2-9, was commanded by God as a prophetic act. Gomer's unfaithfulness to Hosea mirrored Israel's unfaithfulness to God. Despite Gomer's adultery, Hosea was instructed to love and redeem her, symbolizing God's enduring love and covenant faithfulness towards Israel despite their idolatry and disobedience.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 14:22-33, what miracle did Jesus perform when he walked on the water, and what was the reaction of the disciples?

options.text: Jesus calmed the storm, and the disciples were amazed.
Jesus walked on the water, and the disciples were terrified.
Jesus healed a blind man, and the disciples were astonished.
Jesus fed a crowd, and the disciples were grateful.

questions.explanation: According to Matthew 14:22-33, Jesus performed the miracle of walking on the water. The disciples were initially terrified, thinking it was a ghost, but Jesus reassured them, saying 'It is I; do not be afraid.' Peter also attempted to walk on the water but began to sink due to his doubt.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to 1 Samuel 16:1-13, what was the significance of David being anointed by Samuel, and how did it relate to his future leadership?

options.text: It signified David's immediate ascension to the throne.
It marked David's rejection by God.
It indicated God's choice of David to succeed Saul as king.
It was a ritual with no future implications.

questions.explanation: The anointing of David by Samuel, as described in 1 Samuel 16:1-13, signified God's selection of David to succeed Saul as king. This act was a divine endorsement of David's future leadership, though it did not immediately result in his ascension to the throne.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: In the diagram below, a map illustrates Paul's second missionary journey. According to Acts 16:9-10, what was the significance of the Macedonian call for Paul's missionary work?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='180' fill='#f0f0f0'/><text x='160' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Map of Paul's Second Missionary Journey</text></svg>

options.text: It led Paul to abandon his mission to Europe.
It prompted Paul to continue his journey in Asia.
It encouraged Paul to cross into Macedonia and preach the gospel.
It had no impact on Paul's missionary plans.

questions.explanation: The Macedonian call, as recorded in Acts 16:9-10, was a vision Paul received where a man from Macedonia pleaded for help. This vision was interpreted as a divine call to preach the gospel in Macedonia, thus expanding Paul's missionary work into Europe.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 8:4-7, what was Amos' criticism of the Israelites, and what did he emphasize as the consequence of their actions?

options.text: Amos criticized their idolatry and predicted their exile.
Amos condemned their social injustice and foretold their punishment.
Amos denounced their religious hypocrisy and emphasized their need for repentance.
Amos praised their faithfulness and promised their prosperity.

questions.explanation: Amos 8:4-7 records Amos' criticism of the Israelites for their social injustice, particularly their exploitation of the poor. Amos emphasized that God would not forget their deeds and would punish them accordingly.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:21-22, what is Jesus' teaching on anger and its consequences, and how does it relate to the commandment 'You shall not murder'?

options.text: Jesus taught that anger is permissible as long as it does not lead to murder.
Jesus emphasized that anger is as serious as murder in God's eyes.
Jesus stated that murder is worse than anger.
Jesus ignored the commandment against murder.

questions.explanation: In Matthew 5:21-22, Jesus expands on the commandment 'You shall not murder' by teaching that anger towards another person is equally serious. He warns that unjustified anger can lead to judgment, emphasizing the importance of reconciliation.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.subtopic: Sermon on the Mount and Parables
questions.question_text: According to Matthew 5:43-48, what is Jesus' teaching on loving one's enemies, and what does it reveal about the character of God?

options.text: Jesus teaches that loving one's enemies is a sign of weakness and a departure from God's character.
Jesus emphasizes that loving one's enemies is a demonstration of perfection and a reflection of God's character.
Jesus commands that one should only love their neighbors and not their enemies.
Jesus suggests that loving one's enemies is optional and not a requirement for being a true follower.

questions.explanation: Jesus' teaching on loving one's enemies, as recorded in Matthew 5:43-48, emphasizes that this love demonstrates perfection and reflects God's character, who makes His sun rise on the evil and the good. This teaching is a call to imitate God's impartial love and mercy.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.question_text: According to Acts 9:1-31, what was the significance of Paul's conversion experience on the road to Damascus, and how did it impact his mission?
questions.diagram_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M50,100 L270,100' stroke='black' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='20' fill='blue'/></svg>

options.text: Paul's conversion was a minor event that had little impact on his future mission.
Paul's conversion was a dramatic transformation that radically changed his mission from persecuting Christians to spreading the Gospel.
Paul's conversion was not a significant change, as he continued to persecute Christians after Damascus.
Paul's conversion was solely a result of his own efforts and not a divine intervention.

questions.explanation: Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus, as described in Acts 9:1-31, was a pivotal event that transformed him from a persecutor of Christians to a key figure in spreading the Gospel. This dramatic change was a result of a divine intervention, marking the beginning of his missionary journeys.

questions.topic: Old Testament (Creation to Exile)
questions.question_text: According to Amos 5:21-24, what was Amos' criticism of the Israelites' religious practices, and what did he emphasize as the true requirement of God?

options.text: Amos criticized the Israelites for not performing enough religious rituals and emphasized the need for more sacrifices.
Amos praised the Israelites for their religious practices and encouraged them to continue.
Amos criticized the Israelites for their hypocritical religious practices and emphasized that God requires justice and righteousness.
Amos suggested that religious practices were irrelevant to God's requirements.

questions.explanation: Amos 5:21-24 records Amos' criticism of the Israelites' religious practices, condemning their hypocrisy. He emphasized that God rejects their festivals and assemblies, instead requiring justice to roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

questions.topic: New Testament (Life and Ministry of Jesus)
questions.question_text: According to John 11:1-44, what miracle did Jesus perform when he raised Lazarus from the dead, and what was its significance?

options.text: Jesus raised Lazarus to demonstrate His power over nature.
Jesus raised Lazarus to show that He is the Resurrection and the Life, and to foreshadow His own resurrection.
Jesus raised Lazarus as a sign of His anger towards the unbelievers.
Jesus raised Lazarus solely to comfort Martha and Mary.

questions.explanation: The raising of Lazarus, as recorded in John 11:1-44, is a significant miracle that demonstrates Jesus' power over death. It is a sign that Jesus is the Resurrection and the Life and serves as a precursor to His own resurrection, reinforcing His identity as the Son of God.

questions.topic: The Early Church and Paul's Mission
questions.subtopic: Pentecost and the Early Christian Community
questions.question_text: According to Acts 2:1-47, what was the significance of the event of Pentecost for the disciples, and how did it manifest?

options.text: The event of Pentecost was a minor gathering with little impact on the disciples or the early Christian community.
Pentecost marked the beginning of the Church, characterized by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, enabling the disciples to speak in various languages and boldly preach the Gospel.
Pentecost was primarily a celebration of the Jewish harvest festival with no significant impact on the early Christians.
The event of Pentecost was a time of confusion and division among the disciples.

questions.explanation: The event of Pentecost, as described in Acts 2:1-47, was pivotal for the disciples and the early Christian community.
